title: The Old Woman and the King's Elephant

keywords: the tale of the old woman and the king
full_text:
During an imperial procession through the outskirts of Vijayanagara, King Krishnadevaraya’s ceremonial tusker grew excited by the sound of festival drums. The elephant broke away from the procession road and trampled straight through the small vegetable patch belonging to an impoverished widow named Parvatamma, crushing her entire season's crop of brinjals, gourds, and lentils.

The royal officers tossed the old woman two copper coins and rode away, ignoring her weeping.
Heartbroken, Parvatamma came to Tenali Raman’s home, crying that her grandchildren would starve.

Tenali comforted her: 'Mother, King Krishnadevaraya is a righteous king whose officers have acted with callous arrogance. Come with me to the palace tomorrow.'

The next morning, while the King was holding public audience, Tenali entered leading the weeping old woman.
Tenali bowed:
'Maharaj, a grave dispute has arisen regarding a tenant farmer who damaged an imperial property. The court desires to know: if a careless subject destroys a neighbor's livelihood, what is the lawful punishment?'

The King replied with firm authority:
'The law of Vijayanagara is clear! The offender must restore the damage tenfold, and must personally help restore the ruined field with his own hands!'

Tenali smiled with solemn reverence:
'Jahanpanah, your decree is righteous.
Yesterday, your imperial ceremonial tusker trampled through this widow's only vegetable field, destroying her entire year's sustenance, while your officers tossed her two coppers!
According to your royal verdict just spoken, the Emperor must restore her crop tenfold, and provide personal labor to repair her field!'

The courtiers gasped at Tenali’s audacity.
King Krishnadevaraya’s face flushed red, but the Emperor possessed genuine greatness of spirit.
He stood up from his golden throne and descended to the marble floor:
'Tenali is right. A king’s elephant cannot be above the law that protects the poor.'

The King ordered the royal treasury to pay Parvatamma one hundred gold dinars—tenfold the value of her crop—and granted her permanent title to five fertile acres with canal irrigation.
Furthermore, to demonstrate humility before his subjects, the King sent a royal team of bullocks and palace gardeners to plow and sow her new field completely!

Parvatamma blessed the King with tears of joy.
The people of Vijayanagara cheered their Emperor’s justice, while Tenali showed that true loyalty holds a mirror of righteousness before power.
moral: Sovereigns must remember that the humblest citizen’s bread is sacred; royal power owes full restitution for unintended damage.
